Important caveat up front: almost none of these have a clean "T-Mobile per year" number. The frequency and loss figures in your files are mostly national (FBI IC3, FTC), count only complaints filed, and cover all carriers, so T-Mobile's own slice isn't broken out. T-Mobile's actual costs show up as lumpy one-time hits (settlements, fines, awards), not annual run-rates. I'll give you exactly what the files support and flag where a number doesn't exist.

## 1. Account/number takeover (SIM swap, port-out, eSIM)

|                  |                                                                                                                                  |
|------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Measure          | Figure (source)                                                                                                                  |
| Frequency        | SIM-swap complaints to FBI IC3, national: 2,026 (2022) → 1,075 (2023) → 982 (2024) → 971 (2025)                                  |
| People affected  | Complaints only, so true number is higher; T-Mobile share not reported                                                           |
| Cost per year    | National IC3 losses: \$72.65M (2022) → \$48.8M (2023) → \$25.98M (2024) → \$17.37M (2025)                                        |
| Per victim       | ~\$26K average (IC3 2024); tail is huge (Jones, \$38M)                                                                           |
| Cost to T-Mobile | One SIM swap = \$33M arbitration award (Jones, made public March 2025). T-Mobile says successful swaps are down \>99% since 2022 |

The trend is falling in volume but the harm per victim is severe, and a single case can cost T-Mobile more than an FCC fine.

This is the category with the least public data and no customer-facing product, which is why both files flag it as a "large gap."

The files include this as a structural warning: T-Mobile runs the same cloud/CRM/vendor setup, not because of a big T-Mobile-specific loss yet.

## 5. Customer-facing scam texts and calls

|                    |                                                                                                                     |
|--------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Measure            | Figure (source)                                                                                                     |
| Frequency          | FTC: text-scam losses \$470M in 2024, 5x the 2020 level. IC3 phishing/spoofing: 193,407 complaints (2024, national) |
| Volume at T-Mobile | ~3B scam texts blocked in 2025; 50% more scam messages than 2024; 19.8B calls flagged in 2023; 160B+ since 2017     |
| Cost per year      | \$470M is national across all carriers; T-Mobile's customers' share isn't isolated                                  |
| Cost to T-Mobile   | Almost entirely indirect (reputation, churn, support load); no direct annual dollar figure in the files             |

Fastest-growing category, but the cost to T-Mobile is reputational and operational rather than a documented payout.

## The one number that is "T-Mobile per year"

If you add up T-Mobile's documented direct hits, 2021 breach (~![](data:image/png;base64,)60M), FCC decree (![](data:image/png;base64,)33M), that's roughly \$625M over about four years, heavily front-loaded by the 2021 settlement. So a rough, caveat-heavy "~\$150M/year," but it's lumpy and dominated by one event, not a steady rate.

For a pitch, the honest framing is: the measurable money is in \#1 (per-victim catastrophe T-Mobile pays for in court) and \#3 (half-billion-dollar breach settlements), while \#5 is the fastest-rising threat by volume.
